bamboo-fencing-edging.lead: Natural, black, carbonized or mahogany bamboo — supplied as fence rolls, half-round screens, split-slat screening, expandable trellis and border edging. Open any product for full specifications, sizes, photos and answers to common questions.

body.p: Bamboo fencing is one of the quickest ways to add privacy and warmth to a garden, balcony or terrace. Rolled bamboo screening fixes straight onto an existing fence, wall, chain-link, railing or a simple post frame, so an ugly boundary turns into a natural, uniform screen in an afternoon — with no building work and no heavy materials to handle.

We supply bamboo fencing wholesale to importers, garden centres, DIY retailers and landscapers. Every product on this page is made from natural bamboo, without pesticides, formaldehyde or toxic glues, and is held together with galvanised wire rather than adhesives.

body.h3: Which bamboo fence do you need?

body.p: The range covers four kinds of product. Each one solves a different job, so it is worth choosing by use rather than by looks alone.

ul: Bamboo fence rolls — whole canes wired side by side. The all-round choice for garden privacy and for cladding existing fences.
Half-round and split-slat screens — canes split lengthwise, so the screen is lighter, sits flat against a fence and gives a smoother, more refined face.
Expandable bamboo trellis — a lattice that pulls open to size, made for climbing plants, wall decoration and light, open screening.
Bamboo edging — short canes wired into a low border for lawns, flower beds and paths; the version with feet pushes straight into the soil.

body.p: Natural bamboo has a light honey-yellow tone that suits most gardens and mellows slowly outdoors. Natural black bamboo is a species that grows dark, so the colour belongs to the cane itself rather than to a coating. Carbonized bamboo is heat-treated, which gives a warm brown tone that runs through the material. Mahogany bamboo has a reddish-brown finish for a more decorative look. The same finishes are available across rolls, half-round screens, trellis and edging, so a whole project can be matched in one colour.

body.h3: Cane diameter, heights and roll lengths

body.p: Cane diameter decides how solid and how strong the screen is. Fine canes of 14–16 mm give a light screen for edging, balconies and decorative panels. Canes of 20–30 mm and 30–35 mm are the standard for garden privacy fencing. Giant canes of 40–60 mm are used for the half-round screens. Standard heights run from 1.0 to 2.0 m and rolls are usually 1.8 m or 3 m long; custom heights, lengths and diameters are made to order for larger quantities.

body.h3: How long does bamboo fencing last?

body.p: Rolled bamboo screening on an existing fence typically lasts somewhere between 3 and 8 years outdoors, depending on climate, cane thickness and how it is fixed. Thicker canes and carbonized or naturally black bamboo cope best with sun and rain. Every roll is double-stitched with rust-proof galvanised steel wire, so the canes stay tight and straight season after season.

Two simple things make the biggest difference: keep the bottom edge off wet soil and out of standing water, and fix the screen with UV-stable ties or galvanised staples instead of cheap ties that turn brittle in sunlight. Brushing off dirt once a year and letting the screen dry out after long wet spells keeps it looking good for longer.

Unroll the screen along the fence, line it up at the top and fix it every 30–40 cm with ties, galvanised staples or screws through the wire. On open ground, a frame of wooden or metal posts with two horizontal rails gives the screen a firm, straight line. Rolls can be cut to length by cutting the binding wire between two canes, and several rolls can be joined to cover long boundaries.

Bamboo is one of the fastest-growing plants in the world and regrows from its own roots after harvesting, so it can be cut again and again without replanting. It is renewable, biodegradable at the end of its life and needs no chemical treatment to work as a fence — an easy choice for customers who want a natural alternative to plastic, PVC or treated timber screening.

bamboo-fence-panels.lead: From clean fixed panels in natural or black bamboo to hand-built Japanese garden fences — Kumo, Misugaki, Sode-gaki and Koetsu-gaki. Open any panel for full specifications, sizes, photos and answers to common questions.

body.p: Bamboo fence panels are rigid, ready-made sections of bamboo fencing. Where a roll needs an existing fence or frame to hang on, a panel brings its own structure: the canes are fixed into a frame or wired tightly onto rails, so it goes straight between posts and gives a clean, finished edge from day one.

That makes panels the natural choice for new boundaries, gates, garden rooms and feature walls, and for projects where the fence has to look as good as a piece of garden furniture. Every panel is made from natural bamboo, without pesticides, formaldehyde or toxic glues.

body.h3: Fixed panels or Japanese garden fences?

body.p: Fixed bamboo panels are the straightforward option: whole natural or natural black canes in a firm, square panel, for privacy along a boundary, a terrace or a balcony. They give the look of a bamboo fence roll with the stiffness of a panel.
Our Japanese-style panels follow traditional garden fence designs and are built largely by hand. Each style has its own purpose:

ul: Kumo and Misugaki panels — closely set canes in a wooden frame with bamboo cross-rails, for full privacy with a calm, Japanese look.
Lattice-top panels — a solid lower section with an open lattice at the top, so the fence feels lighter while the lower part still screens.
Bamboo branch panels — bamboo twigs packed into a wooden frame, a textured, rustic screen in natural or black.
Sode-gaki sleeve fences — narrow, free-standing accent fences that frame an entrance, a lantern or a view.
Koetsu-gaki wing fences — a curved top and an open diamond lattice, a sculptural piece for garden features and low divisions.

body.p: Panels come in standard sizes for each style, from low accent pieces to full-height privacy panels, and custom widths and heights are made to order. Finishes include natural yellow bamboo, natural black bamboo and carbonized bamboo, combined with dark-stained wooden frames on the Japanese styles. Open a panel to see its exact sizes, thickness and weight.

Bamboo panels fix between wooden or metal posts with screws or brackets, or straight onto an existing fence or wall. Set the posts first, check the spacing against the panel width, and leave a small gap at the bottom so the panel stays clear of wet soil. Sleeve and wing fences stand on their own posts and are often used singly, as a finishing touch rather than a full boundary.

body.h3: How long do bamboo fence panels last?

body.p: Framed panels usually outlast rolled screening, because the canes are held firmly in the frame and kept off the ground. Placed on posts with good drainage underneath, and cleaned and dried off now and then, a bamboo panel keeps its shape and colour for many seasons. Carbonized and naturally black bamboo are the most weather-resistant options.

reed-fencing.lead: From budget fine reed to top-quality extra-thick — peeled, unpeeled, split and Japanese-style reed fencing. Open any version for full specifications, sizes, photos and answers to common questions.

body.p: Reed fencing is natural reed stems laid side by side and bound with wire into a flexible roll. It is light, easy to handle and gives instant privacy with a soft, natural texture — on an existing fence, a balcony railing, a wall or a simple post frame. Because it lets some air through, it also breaks the wind rather than catching it like a solid screen.

We supply reed fencing wholesale to importers, garden centres, DIY chains and landscapers. Every roll is made from 100% natural reed, without pesticides or chemical treatments, and is bound with rust-proof wire.

Peeled reed has its outer leaf removed, which leaves a smooth, even, light-yellow surface — the clean, refined choice for modern gardens and balconies. Unpeeled reed keeps the natural leaf sheath, so it looks more rustic and varied in colour and is often a little more economical. Both are available in several stem thicknesses, and carbonized reed adds a warmer, deeper tone.
Stem thickness decides how dense, how strong and how private the fence is:

ul: Fine reed, 3–6 mm — a light, economical screen; the high-density version packs the stems tightly for more privacy.
Thick reed, 5–8 mm — the all-round grade for garden privacy, sturdy and even.
Extra-thick reed, 8–10 mm — the strongest and most solid grade, with the best privacy and the longest life.

body.p: Next to the standard rolls we make split reed fencing, a Japanese-style reed fence with bamboo rails and an Italian-style peeled reed fence, each with its own look and binding.
Standard rolls are 3 m, 5 m or 6 m long, in heights from 1.0 to 2.0 m. Other heights and lengths are made to order for larger quantities, and each version page lists its exact sizes.

body.h3: How long does reed fencing last?

body.p: In a normal European garden, reed fencing lasts at least 3–5 years outdoors, and the thicker grades often longer. Reed is one of the lightest natural fencing materials and its natural yellow colour changes very little over the years. To get the most out of it, keep the bottom edge off wet ground, fix it tightly so it cannot flap in the wind, and let it dry out after long rainy periods.

Unroll the reed along the fence or railing and fix it every 30–40 cm with UV-stable cable ties, wire or galvanised staples. On open ground, put up posts with a top and bottom rail and fix the reed to the rails. A roll can be shortened by cutting the binding wire, and rolls can be joined end to end for long runs.

Shade on pergolas, carports and garden structures.
